 The present editors are less certain about this reading, where the MS is all but impossible
to decipher decisively. GM’s third gloss, however, is much more convincing, and also more
critical to his argument for a fast-developing and potentially sexual relationship between S.
and Jane Williams. Written in a tiny but quite emphatic hand between two of TL’s closing
lines is a phrase convincingly read by GM as Alas I kiss you Jane. Donald Reiman in BSM
i 269 reads this as ‘Alas I kiss you [?]’, commenting in his ‘Notes on the Manuscript and
the Transcription’ that ‘the significance of this obscure phrase was discussed by GMM [i.e.
GM] in RES . . . and disputed by DHR in PMLA’ (BSM i 315). Reiman’s reference is to his
article ‘Shelley’s ‘The Triumph of Life’: The Biographical Problem’, PMLA lxxviii (1963)
